chapter_theme: The two princes Vijayan and Tivittan are born, grow into youth and set the city's women aflame, and the king rises, is blessed and goes in state to the assembly hall.

cast.role: the elder prince, born to the first queen
the younger prince, born to the second queen
the queen who bears Vijayan (unnamed in these verses)
the queen who bears Tivittan (unnamed in these verses)
the gods who rain flowers at the birth
the city's young women who love the princes
the king, father of the two princes
the armed young guards who come to the king
the women attendants who praise and fan the king
the brahmins who bless and crown the king
the sword-bearing chamberlains who guard the king

70.reading: Two beings come down together from the heaven of the kalpa into the queens' wombs and are born, shining like the sea's deep water.
70.nuance: The two are heavenly beings born here, so the story opens their human lives with a rebirth, not a beginning; line 1's திருவயிற்று (holy wombs, plural) shows two mothers.
70.event: Two beings descend from a heavenly kalpa and are born as the two sons of the king.

71.reading: The great queen's joy overflows as Vijayan is born, bright as a white moon that fills the cool world.
71.event: Vijayan is born to the queen.

72.reading: In due time the second queen bears Tivittan, whose radiance outshines the jewel-lights, and the gods rain flowers.
72.nuance: Line 3 has the sea's conches swelling, so earth and heaven both mark the birth.
72.event: Tivittan is born to the second queen, and the gods shower flowers.

73.reading: At their birth the quarters grow clear, the gods' city rings with praise, wishes are fulfilled and the clinging moisture of afflicting evil deeds dries up for many, the poet reports.
73.nuance: The closing என்பவே (they say) gives the claim as report. தீவினைப் பசை pictures karma as a moisture that makes deeds stick; the verse does not say whose deeds, only that it dries for many.
73.event: At the princes' birth the quarters clear and the hold of evil karma is said to dissolve.

claims.claim: the birth of a great being dries up the clinging residue of harmful deeds for many

74.reading: The two grow up in their splendid city and reach the age of princes, and the love-god sets his arrow-buds in the hearts of dark-eyed women.
74.event: The princes come of age and Kaman plants his arrows in the women's hearts.

75.reading: A prince is described: fragrant with conch-white, lotus-petal eyes, a crest like dark night, gold earrings swinging at his ears.
75.nuance: The sequence of 75 and 76 describes the elder, as 78 later names the other as his younger.

76.reading: The elder prince has an unwithering garland, broad chest, long arms, shining body, shoulders like hill peaks and a stately walk.

77.reading: The younger prince is described: body like a fresh flower, eyes surpassing lotus, red lips like the ambal, and the holy mark on his chest.
77.nuance: திருமறு is the mark on the chest; the verse gives it as a feature of the person without comment.

78.reading: The younger prince bears the emblems of conch and discus on his palm, walks like a splendid elephant, and is the younger of the one just described.
78.nuance: Conch (சங்கு) and discus (திகிரி) on the palm are given as body marks. 109 later has the court declare Tivittan a guardian of the whole world, which makes these marks read as signs of rule.

79.reading: As the princes enter a youth that sets fire in the hearts of bangled women, their splendour dulls their rivals' wealth.
79.event: The princes reach an age that kindles love-sickness in women.

80.reading: The coral-lipped women turn glances at them, as if the love-god's flower-arrows had taken shape in sidelong looks.
80.nuance: அவர்கடம் மருள்கொலோ (is it their bewilderment?) leaves open whether the glance is love or the princes' charm striking them.
80.event: The women show their love by glances, which the poet likens to Kaman's arrows.

81.reading: The women swoon with fear: the dark-gemmed one has come in a dream, taken their hearts and will not let go; will he take their lives?
81.nuance: The dark one of the sea's colour (81) and the conch-coloured one (82) are likely the two princes, as 106 later calls the younger கடல் வண்ணன்; the verse itself names neither.
81.event: The women, dazed, say a prince seen in dream has taken their hearts.

82.reading: One woman says the conch-coloured prince is in her heart and not a target for other women's eyes; the poet asks who raised this heart-sickness, and answers that it is their age.
82.nuance: Lines 1-2 are the woman's thought, lines 3-4 the poet's question, so the speaker changes within the verse; 82's assignment is uncertain.
82.event: A woman declares that the fair prince lives in her heart.

83.reading: For the women the fire of desire rises within for these radiant youths and burns with countless flames, and no creature but shame-bound women bears it more heavily.
83.nuance: காம வூழெரி joins desire and ஊழ், a fire from fate; the last line reads as a claim that women bound by shame suffer most, but its sense is unsure.

84.reading: Because the heart-sickness that goes out to the wealthy lords grows stronger in each woman than the other, the princes reach the age that makes a fire burn in their hearts.
84.nuance: This verse repeats 79's closing line, now attaching the fire to the lords' wealth (திருவளர் செல்வர்) as well as to their youth.

85.reading: On another day the crowned king, his head ringed with flowers and bees, passes his rest among the young women of his court.
85.nuance: The sense of இளையவர் குழைய (the young [women/men] drooping) is not clear from the verse.
85.event: The king rests in his palace among the young women.

86.reading: In the garland-hall amid the smoke of aloe and honey, the king on a cotton-stuffed couch gives himself to rest until the red light changes.
86.nuance: செஞ்சுடர் இரிவதோர் திறத்தனாயினான் is hard; it is read here as the king stirring as the red light moves.
86.event: The king sleeps in the garland-hall until dawn.

87.reading: The king wakes and signals, and young attendants, in gold clothes, tight girdles and with bows in hand, come to take their post at his feet.
87.event: Armed young attendants come to guard the awakened king.

88.reading: Ceremonial articles gather by him, he washes his eyes, and the lotus-faced women call out their wish for him to live many years.
88.nuance: Line 1's தவழழொளி தடாவி is a doubtful reading.
88.event: The king washes his eyes and the women wish him long life.

89.reading: Brahmins bless him, set the flower-crown on his head, and he bows to the gods and praises them like Indra.
89.nuance: The verse puts brahmin blessing and the king's worship before the day's rule begins, as part of the morning rite.
89.event: Brahmins bless and crown the king, who then worships the gods.

90.reading: Women with garlands and staves go before the king through the palace gate, with the drum's roar, and he plans to reach the assembly hall.
90.event: The king, escorted, sets out for the assembly hall.

91.reading: Girls praise his golden feet, fan him with chowries and clothing, and the king reaches the great outer court.
91.event: The king, praised and fanned by girls, reaches the outer court.

92.reading: Chamberlains with swords and girdles guard the king, lord of the Naga-poisoned (poison-spear-bearing) city, as he goes.
92.nuance: நஞ்சிவர் வேனர பதியை in line 2 is hard; it is read as an epithet of the king.
92.event: Chamberlains guard the king as he passes.

93.reading: The king passes the three gates, scented with water and strewn with flowers, and reaches the pavilion outside.
93.event: The king passes three gates and reaches the outer pavilion.

94.reading: The king enters the great hall of crystal, gold and coral pillars that shines like heaven's wealth.
94.nuance: Line 3 begins டுளொங்கொளி, an apparent misprint for துளங்கொளி.
94.event: The king enters the assembly hall.

links.note: At the princes' birth the clinging moisture of evil deeds is said to dry up for many; Kural 5 says deeds of darkness do not cling to those who delight in the Lord's praise.
links.teaches: The Kural lifts the hold of deeds through the devotee's own praise, but the epic lifts it for many through the birth of a great being, so each work places the loosening of karma somewhere different.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a stated condition for karma's loosening, the devotee's praise, which it does not state.
gains.b: Kural 5 gets a case where the hold is loosened by someone else's birth and not by the sufferer's devotion, a test of how exclusive its condition is.

links.note: Both verses close on the princes reaching an age that sets a fire in the women's hearts; 79 puts the cause in their youth, and 84 adds the women's sickness for wealthy lords.
links.teaches: The repeated line first locates the fire in the princes' youth, then ties it to wealth and rank, so the same phrase shifts what the women are said to burn for.

links.note: 78 lists conch and discus on the younger prince's palm; in 109 the court names him one who will guard the whole world under one umbrella.
links.teaches: The body marks listed as ornament in 78 are read, in 109, as a sign of universal rule, which changes how the earlier portrait should be heard.

links.note: 79 shows youth as a fire kindled in women; Tirumanthiram 180 has a man recall being sweet as cane juice to women and now bitter as the kanjiram fruit.
links.teaches: The epic shows only the rising stage of desire's arc, and Tirumular supplies the other end, so together they place the princes' present blaze on a curve that ends in the speaker's bitterness.

gains.a: The epic's fire of youth gets the end of its arc, which the verse does not show.
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 180 gets the beginning of its curve, the stage and the women's fire from which its speaker later falls.

links.note: 80 likens the women's sidelong glances to Kaman's arrows; Naladiyar 17 warns against desiring a woman of spear-like eyes, for she too will lean on a staff.
links.teaches: The epic shows the glance as a weapon at the moment of its force, and Naladiyar names the later fall of the same weapon, so the pair sets the glance's power against its short life.

gains.a: The epic's glances get a limit it does not state, that the spear-eyed will stoop and walk with a staff.
gains.b: Naladiyar 17 gets a scene of the spear-like glance at work, so its warning is aimed at what the reader has just watched.

source_issues: 77: line 2 repaired in the source, TSCII leftover ு + U+0BA1 read as ூ.
88: line 1 தவழழொளி தடாவி has a doubled letter and may be corrupt.
92: line 2 நஞ்சிவர் வேனர பதியை is hard to construe.
94: line 3 begins டுளொங்கொளி, probably a misprint for துளங்கொளி.
